chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding

regarding a man who struck with his sword a camel or a sheep in other than its (proper) slaughter place, and had named (said Bismillah) when he struck. So he said: It is not permissible to eat a slaughtered animal that is not slaughtered from its (proper) slaughter place — meaning when one is deliberate in that and his state is not a state of necessity. But as for when he is compelled to do so and what he intends to slaughter proves difficult for him, then there is no problem with that.

key_terms.اضْطِرَار: State of necessity or compulsion — a legal concept that lifts prohibitions in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.ذَبِيحَة: A slaughtered animal — one that has been ritually slaughtered according to Islamic law
key_terms.سَمَّى: Saying Bismillah (naming God) at the moment of slaughter — a required condition for the slaughter to be valid
key_terms.مَذْبَح: The proper place of slaughter — for a camel, the jugular notch (nahr); for sheep and cattle, the throat (dhabh)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat an animal slaughtered at the wrong place if Bismillah was said?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) addresses a jurisprudential question about an animal struck with a sword at a non-standard slaughter site. The ruling distinguishes two cases: when the act is deliberate, the animal is not permissible to eat; but when there is genuine necessity or the animal becomes unruly and difficult to slaughter properly, the act is valid and the animal is permissible. This reflects the Islamic legal principle that necessity (idtirār) can lift otherwise prohibited acts, as codified in fiqh.
